title: Architecture & Codebase Orientation
text: mysterycall provides common functions mystery-caller / audit studies measure patient access care — studies trained callers contact provider offices different insurance scenarios (e.g. Medicaid vs. commercial plan) record whether appointment offered long wait . package covers whole arc: Build provider roster — NPI/taxonomy search, address normalization, academic classification, census/geography enrichment. Clean validate call log — one row per call, insurance arm recorded outcomes. Analyze — acceptance-rate disparities wait-time models (Poisson / NB / logistic / linear mixed models), appropriate clustering CIs. Report — publication-ready tables, STROBE flow diagrams, prose “results-section” sentences, plus verifiable provenance trail.

what: 2. The big picture: a two-phase pipeline

title: Architecture & Codebase Orientation
text: @family tag function authoritative grouping (drives pkgdown reference sections). major families, largest first: outcomes — analytic core: acceptance rates, wait-time models (poisson_model, nb_model, logistic_model, lmm), IRR/GMR helpers, power-analysis simulators (nb_power, marginal_power, …). provider / npi / census / address-normalization / academic-indicators — everything turns specialty + geography validated provider roster. data / data-preparation / data-quality / quality / validation / safe-joins — cleaning, de-duplication, flagging, joins refuse silently drop rows. manuscript / reporting / table / green-journal-* — publication output: results_paragraph, Table 1, disparities tables, docx/flextable export, STROBE flow, “Green Journal” (Obstetrics & Gynecology) themed figures. workflow / logging / progress / utilities — orchestration cross-cutting helpers (structured logging, progress spinners, small utilities). adding function, pick family belongs file matching _pkgdown.yml section.

what: 5. The documentation model (read this before touching any R/ doc)
title: Architecture & Codebase Orientation
text: Roxygen comments live R/, generated man/*.Rd files checked repo must stay sync. canonical workflow : Consequences contributors: Always run document() editing #' block function signature. CI run ; drifted .Rd real R CMD check WARNING (codoc / undocumented-arguments). @family bidirectional. Adding @family outcomes function makes roxygen rewrite “outcomes:” cross-reference every outcomes .Rd. Never hand-edit lists — regenerate. Internal helpers use @noRd (man page) — named leading dot (.mc_*, .fmt_*). Exported functions mysterycall_* carry @param, @return, least one @examples. Examples need network/API heavy optional package wrapped \dontrun{} / @examplesIf requireNamespace(...).
code: devtools::document()   # regenerates man/*.Rd and NAMESPACE from the @ tags

title: Architecture & Codebase Orientation
text: non-obvious, project-specific rules — things newcomer trips : Naming. Exported = mysterycall_<verb>(). Internal = dotted (.mc_format_p, .wilson_ci). Deprecated shims live R/deprecated.R. Input validation. Prefer checkmate::assert_*; stopifnot() used carries named message: stopifnot("datamust data frame" = .data.frame(data)). Optional dependencies. Anything Suggests (ggplot2, survival, lme4, glmmTMB, mice, sf, tidycensus, gt, …) guarded requireNamespace("pkg", quietly = TRUE) first use — never library() inside function. RNG hygiene. Functions need seed use withr::local_seed(seed), set.seed(), don’t clobber caller’s global random stream. Locale-independent reproducibility. Sorts whose result affects output — model’s reference level, provenance hash’s key order — use sort(..., method = "radix") don’t depend LC_COLLATE. phase-2 column contract. run_workflow() renames incoming columns short “standard” names (reason_for_exclusions → exclusion_reasons). run_analysis() documents long names defaults tolerates short aliases via .mc_resolve_col() — two chain cleanly. add column parameter touch, wire helper. P-values. .mc_format_p() (R/format_pvalue.R) single source truth p-value strings tables ("< 0.001" / "0.043"). Manuscript prose uses spaced "p < 0.001" / "p = 0.043" convention. Wait-time outcome. canonical wait-time column business_days_until_appointment; calendar_days documented secondary column calendar-vs-business sensitivity.

title: Architecture & Codebase Orientation
text: test-<name>.R mirrors R/<name>.R; testthat edition 3, run parallel (Config/testthat/parallel: true). Label pattern: test_that("fn: case → expected", ...). Guard tests needing Suggests package skip_if_not_installed("pkg"). Every test_that must actually assert — empty “doesn’t error” blocks; use expect_no_error() really assertion. use skip_on_cran() hide failing test.

what: 8. Adding a new function, end to end
title: Architecture & Codebase Orientation
text: Create R/<name>.R. Add roxygen: @family <group>, @param, @return, @seealso related functions, least one @examples. devtools::document() generate man/<name>.Rd update NAMESPACE. File function right _pkgdown.yml reference section. Add tests/testthat/test-<name>.R — happy path + NA/empty input. Add NEWS.md bullet current dev version. devtools::check() → 0 errors / 0 warnings.

title: Architecture & Codebase Orientation
text: analysis spine: R/run_analysis.R — shows step model, validation, outcome subsystems called. model, end end: R/poisson_model.R (R/lmm.R) — fitting, reference-level pick, IRR/GMR tables, print() method. Reporting: R/results_paragraph.R — model output becomes sentence. Provenance: R/clean_phase_1_results.R (writer) R/audit-verify.R (reader) — audit-trail hash verification. Collection: R/run_mystery_caller_workflow.R — phase-1/phase-2 flow. Questions aren’t answered belong GitHub Issue.

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Suggested fix order: 5, 6, 1 (wrong numbers/IDs data & manuscript) → 7, 8, 16 (paired-design math) → 15, 19 (ZIP leading zeros) → 9–14 (reporting/stat correctness) → 2, 3 (generalization + rebuild) → 17–21, 4.

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: paired insurance design (NPI called insurances) mishandled power/sensitivity machinery — nb_power.R (#7) simulates unpaired, sensitivity_both_insurance.R (#8) tests unpaired, power_analysis.R (#16) double-counts calls. Consequence study planning: pre-specified power targets miscomputed (overstate required N within-physician comparison). ZIP leading zeros — normalize_zip5 (#15) extract_zip5 (#19) disagree padding; unifying left-pad--coercion fixes . Silent data loss ~9 Northeast states/territories. Manuscript-facing functions can print flatly wrong claims — “p = 0” (#6), unconditional “significantly associated” (#13), reversed forest-plot significance colors (#12), abs()-collapsed CIs (#1). go straight paper.

what: 1 — irr_to_days.R:187–192, 197 — abs() on CI bounds hides zero-crossing (and reverses order)
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Status: broken source installed 1.6.0. $table computes signed day-CI (days_ci_lower/upper) correctly, sentence builder abs_lo <- abs(days_ci_lower), abs_hi <- abs(days_ci_upper) printing. Failure (real ENT output): Facial Plastics true days CI = [−6.5, +11.4] (crosses zero, p=0.852) prints “95% CI 6.5 11.4 days” — null result rendered positive bounded effect. IRR < 1 bounds negative → abs() flips sign reverses order. Fix: drop abs(); print signed bounds (formatC(..., flag="+")). Bounds already ordered (days_ci_lower < days_ci_upper). Optionally append “(significant)” CI spans 0.

what: 5 — clean_phase_1_results.R:226 — missing NPI becomes the string "NA", defeating the missing-NPI fallback
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: format() renders NA literal "NA" (verified). Every downstream .na(.data$npi) check (lines ~299–308, 420–424) always FALSE rows. Failure: input npi = c("1234567893", NA) → column becomes c("1234567893","NA"). missing-NPI row gets random_id (random_id="NA"), original_npi="NA", doctor_id = coalesce(npi, random_id) = "NA". missing-NPI rows collapse doctor_id="NA" collide downstream joins — exact placeholder-collision package claims prevent. completeness_npi also miscounts present. Fix: keep real NA: ifelse(.na(v), NA_character_, trimws(format(v, scientific=FALSE, trim=TRUE))).
code: phase1_data[[npi_col_before_clean]] <- trimws(format(phase1_data[[npi_col_before_clean]],                                                      scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: <0.001 guard. p < 5e-4 rounds 0. Failure: true p = 3e-8 → sentence reads “p-value Medicaid vs BCBS 0.” Fix: p_txt <- (p_raw < 0.001) "< 0.001" else formatC(p_raw, digits = digits_p, format = "f"); never render round()ed p format().

what: 7 — nb_power.R:92–108 — paired design simulated as unpaired (overstates required N)
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Docstring: calls_per_physician “Default 2L (one Medicaid, one reference insurance)” — within-physician comparison. loop draws two disjoint physician sets (u_ref R1..Rn, u_trt T1..Tn) gives every physician’s calls one insurance → insurance simulated clusters. random intercept inflates ins SE. Failure: mysterycall_nb_power(36, irr=0.75) reports power/N unpaired 72-physician design (total_n = 144), systematically overstating N paired study needs. Fix: one physician set called arms; single u per physician added ; ins varies within physician.

what: 8 — sensitivity_both_insurance.R:143–146 — unpaired test on a paired design
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Physicians selected called Medicaid BCBS, compared unpaired Welch t.test(outcome ~ insurance), ignoring pairing. Failure: 30 physicians within-physician-correlated waits → unpaired test inflates SE, returns n.s. even paired difference clearly significant. Fix: paired test per-physician differences (t.test(medicaid, bcbs, paired=TRUE) reshaping) mixed model.

what: 9 — model_mae_rmse.R:310–311 — exp() used to invert log1p() (should be expm1())
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: LMM stores log1p(days) (lmm.R:202,213). Back-transform exp(actual_raw) = days + 1. Failure: 20-day wait → reported actual = 21; -day (0-day) appointment → 1, since ’s longer == 0 ’s wrongly kept MAPE denominator, biasing MAPE. (MAE/RMSE/R² unaffected +1 cancels.) Fix: expm1(actual_raw), expm1(predicted_raw).

what: 10 — univariate_lmm_screen.R:135–137 — exp() of a linear coefficient labeled “IRR”
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Model lmerTest::lmer raw days, code reports irr <- exp(coef), exp(coef ± 1.96 SE). Failure: predictor adds +7 days → reported IRR = exp(7) ≈ 1096 fed forest plots. Fix: report additive estimate + estimate ± 1.96 SE mean difference; fit Poisson/NB IRR wanted.

what: 11 — interaction_screen.R:151–163 — interaction significance = min(p) over ALL coefficients
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: P_Value per pair min() every non-intercept coefficient, including two main effects — pair flagged “significant interaction” whenever main effect significant. (Sibling screen_interactions.R filters : terms correctly.) Failure: y ~ insurance * gender, insurance main p<0.001 interaction p=0.7 → reported significant interaction. Fix: restrict p_vals rows whose names contain ":" min().

what: 12 — irr_plot.R:111, 122 — significance colors permuted relative to rows
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: color = tbl$.sig[order(.integer(tbl$term))]; term just re-leveled rev(term), .integer(term) decreasing order() reverse permutation. ggplot binds manual (non-aes) color vector rows existing order. Failure: terms ,B,C p = 0.01,0.5,0.5 (red,navy,navy) → colors applied navy,navy,red; significant drawn non-significant, non-significant C drawn significant. Fix: pass color = tbl$.sig unpermuted, aes(color=.sig) + scale_color_identity().

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Intro sentence asserts significance regardless p-values. (second, correctly-gated definition exists manuscript_helpers.R:269 — two collide; reviewed one overstates.) Failure: table p > 0.2 still opens “insurance significantly associated appointment acceptance.” Fix: gate (matched$p_value < alpha, na.rm = TRUE) → “” vs “significantly”.

what: 14 — icc.R:219 — CI label prints n_boot instead of confidence level
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Object never stores conf_level (structure list 110–121); print method fills "%d%% CI" round(x$n_boot). Failure: print(mysterycall_icc(fit, n_boot=500, conf_level=0.95)) → “500% CI = […]”. Fix: store conf_level object; use round(x$conf_level*100) label, keep n_boot replicate count.

what: 15 — address_normalizer.R:371 (mysterycall_normalize_zip5) — numeric ZIP loses leading zero → NA
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: z <- stringr::str_extract(.character(zip), "\\d{5}"). @param/@examples support numeric input, numeric ZIP leading zero 4 digits → 5-digit run → NA. Failure (verified): normalize_zip5(7001) → NA ("07001"); blanks ZIP CT/MA//NH/NJ/RI/VT/PR/VI normalize_address_df(). Fix: coerce + left-pad extracting, mirroring extract_zip5: sprintf("%05.0f", zip) numerics, strip non-digits formatC(width=5, flag="0").

what: 3 — overdispersion_test.R:159–186 — NB-aware fix in source but not shipped
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Source is_nb/is_mixed branch (“normal NB models”); installed 1.6.0 lacks prints “Underdispersion detected (phi=%s). Model may overfit.” Failure: correct NB GLMM (residual φ=0.72 absorbing Poisson φ=6.22), installed package advises removing predictors. Fix: primarily rebuild + version bump source fix ships. what: 16 — power_analysis.R:172–174 — unpaired branch doubles call count
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: both_arms = FALSE sets n_total_calls <- n_total * 2L, unpaired = one call per provider calls = providers = n_total. Failure: poisson_power(irr=1.4, lambda_ref=14, both_arms=FALSE), n_per_arm=63 → reports n_total_calls=252 (correct: 126). (both_arms=TRUE branch correct.) Fix: n_total_calls <- n_total else branch.

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: outcome_label = "IRR (95 95% CI)" (duplicated “95”) becomes gt column header. Fix: "IRR (95% CI)".

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)

what: 19 — address_utils.R:32–38 (mysterycall_extract_zip5) — dropped-zero + ZIP+4 grabs a +4 digit
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: substr(digits, 1, 5) crosses 5/+4 boundary 5-digit part already lost leading zero. Failure (verified): extract_zip5("7001-1234") → "70011" ("07001"). Bare "00501", "8020", "07001-1234" fine. Fix: strip -+4 suffix first (sub("-.*$","",s)) taking first 5 digits.

what: 20 — impute_age.R:70–78 — near-future graduation year yields a bogus age
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)

Failure: impute_age(2027, ref_year=2026) → 2026-2027+27 = 26, 26 >= min_age(25) → returns 26 (physician hasn’t graduated). Fix: age[grad_year > ref_year] <- NA_integer_ explicitly.

what: 21 — clean_phase_1_results.R:348–370 — non-duplicate mode assigns insurance by row parity

what: 4 — overdispersion_test.R — φ ignores random-effect df for GLMMs (doc caveat)

what: 22 — exclusion_summary.R:234–236 — “included” is a residual that absorbs unrecognized rows
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: inclusion_value validated never used; n_included = total − n_unreachable − n_excluded_among_reached. reason 6 known strings (typo/NA/) silently counted reached+included. what: 36 — prepare_calls.R:144, 163–189 — drop branch injects phantom NA rows

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)

Failure (verified): “Indiana University School Medicine” → IMG ("india"); “University New Mexico” → IMG ("mexico"); “Western University Health Sciences” (US ) → CAN_MD. title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Regression y=group2, x=group1; finite crossover needs slope 0<m<1, beyond crossover y−x=(m−1)x+b < 0 → group2 waits shorter. Sentence/docs say group2 longer. Failure: m=0.5,b=3 → crossover 6; x=10, y=8<10 (group2 shorter), yet prints “[group2] patients experienced longer waits.” Fix: beyond crossover ’s group1 longer wait; fix sentence + @details.

title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: Splits first comma, treats remainder suffix; “Last, First” (documented format) misroutes. Failure: "Smith, John" → first=“Smith”, last=NA, suffix=“John”; "Garcia, Robert, MD" → first=“Garcia”, suffix=“Robert, MD”. Fix: treat post-comma segment suffix matches suffix/credential pattern; else pass whole string humaniformat::parse_names().

what: 44 — lmm.R:340–341, 349–350 — Wald CI (z) vs Satterthwaite p (t-df) mismatch
title: mysterycall — bug report (for fixing)
text: CI uses qnorm z; p uses lmerTest Satterthwaite Pr(>|t|). small residual df disagree; gmr_table inherits. Failure: est=2, se=1, df=8 → z-CI [0.04, 3.96] (excludes 0) Satterthwaite p=0.081. Fix: qt(1-(1-conf_level)/2, df=df_values) per term.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: core exposure mystery-caller study insurance type presented simulated patient. physicians identical: academic-center otolaryngologist, rural solo practitioner, urban multispecialty group physician may systematically different scheduling patterns regardless insurance. differences large unaccounted , become residual variance — noise makes harder detect insurance effect care . Adding physician-level covariates two things simultaneously: Controls confounding. Estimates insurance IRR become precise model accounts reasons wait times differ across physicians nothing insurance. Reduces residual variance. covariate explains variance outcome, unexplained (residual) variance shrinks. Smaller residual variance means narrower confidence intervals greater statistical power — may need fewer physicians follow-study. trade-degrees freedom: every covariate add costs parameters, parameters need data estimate reliably.

what: What is a degree of freedom?
title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: fixed-effect term regression model uses one degree freedom. continuous predictor (age, years practice) uses 1. categorical predictor kk levels uses k−1k - 1 (one level absorbed reference category). model pp total parameters, n−pn - presidual degrees freedom — information left estimate error parameters fitted. Residual df must positive; model becomes singular equals zero.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: Poisson regression assumes mean = variance. Real wait-time data routinely violates : physician busy weeks slow others show variance far exceeding mean (physician effect random intercept alone doesn’t absorb). overdispersion. overdispersion ratio ϕ\phi computed Pearson χ2\chi^2 / residual df. value near 1 means Poisson variance assumption holds. Values > 2 indicate problematic overdispersion.

code: result <- mysterycall_poisson_model(   mc_data,   outcome          = "wait_days",   predictors       = c("insurance"),   random_intercept = "npi" ) result$overdispersion #> [1] 3.47 #> Warning: Overdispersion detected (phi = 3.47). Standard errors may be #>   underestimated. Consider a negative binomial model.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: Switch mysterycall_nb_model(). negative binomial distribution adds dispersion parameter θ\theta (theta) : Var(Y)=μ+μ2θ\text{Var}(Y) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta} θ→∞\theta \\infty, variance equals mean (Poisson). θ→0\theta \0, distribution becomes overdispersed. NB model estimates θ\theta data absorbs excess variance rather fixed-effect standard errors. mysterycall_nb_model() warns : θ<1\theta < 1: extreme overdispersion even NB — consider zero-inflated model. Residual ϕ>2\phi > 2 NB fit: NB model still underfits — investigate zero-inflation outlying observations. θ>100\theta > 100: minimal overdispersion — Poisson model probably adequate; compare AIC.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: recommended multilevel negative binomial model physician covariates : log⁡(μij)=β0+β1Medicaidij+β2Incontinenceij+β3Prolapseij+β4Maleij+β5Academicij+β6Ruralij+∑k=212γkACOGDistrictkij+uj\log(\mu_{ij}) = \beta_0   + \beta_1 \text{Medicaid}_{ij}   + \beta_2 \text{Incontinence}_{ij}   + \beta_3 \text{Prolapse}_{ij}   + \beta_4 \text{Male}_{ij}   + \beta_5 \text{Academic}_{ij}   + \beta_6 \text{Rural}_{ij}   + \sum_{k=2}^{12} \gamma_k \text{ACOGDistrict}_{kij}   + u_j : Yij∼NegBin(μij,θ)Y_{ij} \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu_{ij}, \theta) ii = individual mystery call, jj = physician NPI β0\beta_0 = intercept (log expected wait reference group: BCBS + Bladder pain, female, private, urban, District ) β1\beta_1 = log IRR Medicaid vs BCBS β2,β3\beta_2, \beta_3 = log IRR scenario vs. Bladder Pain β4\beta_4 = log IRR male vs. female physician β5\beta_5 = log IRR Academic vs. Private Practice β6\beta_6 = log IRR Rural vs. Urban γk\gamma_k = fixed effect ACOG District kk (District reference) uj∼𝒩(0,σu2)u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2) = physician-level random intercept Total fixed-effect parameters: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 11 = 18 parameters safe n≥180n \geq 180 observations (EPV = 10).

what: Effect on power: how covariates reduce required sample size
title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: Adding covariates genuinely explain variance outcome reduces residual standard deviation σ\sigma. power formula detecting IRR δ\delta approximately: n≈2σ2(zα/2+zβ)2(log⁡δ)2n \approx \frac{2\sigma^2 (z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2}{(\log \delta)^2} covariate reduces σ\sigma 15%, required nn falls ≈28%\approx 28\% (1−0.8521 - 0.85^2). Approximate power analysis: detecting 25% IRR difference (80% power, α = 0.05), assuming baseline SD ≈ 30 days. Important caveats: R² figures estimates. Whether given covariate actually explains 10% 2% variance depends data. Check 1 - (residual variance covariate) / (residual variance without) fitting models. Adding covariate explains little variance increases parameters without reducing noise — effectively hurting power. EPV constraint binding: adding covariate drops EPV 10, need physicians can include .

Derive physician covariates mc_data$practice_setting <- mysterycall_classify_practice_setting(mc_data$org_name) mc_data$urbanicity       <- mysterycall_classify_ruca(mc_data$ruca_code) mc_data$acog_district    <- mysterycall_assign_region(mc_data$state, type = "acog")  # 3. Fit base Poisson to check overdispersion base_poi <- mysterycall_poisson_model(   mc_data, "wait_days",   predictors       = c("insurance", "scenario"),   random_intercept = "npi" ) base_poi$overdispersion  # if > 2, switch to NB  # 4. Fit NB with covariates nb_full <- mysterycall_nb_model(   mc_data, "wait_days",   predictors       = c("insurance", "scenario",                         "practice_setting", "urbanicity", "acog_district"),   random_intercept = "npi" ) # EPV and overdispersion warnings fire automatically if thresholds are crossed  # 5. Compare models mysterycall_select_best_model(   list(poisson_base = base_poi, nb_full = nb_full),   method = "AIC" )  # 6. Report results print(nb_full) mysterycall_irr_plot(nb_full) mysterycall_write_results_paragraph(nb_full, ref_group = "BCBS", exposure_col = "insurance")

code: adjudicate <- function(raw_appointment, raw_contacted, label_a, label_b) {   agree <- !is.na(label_a) & !is.na(label_b) & label_a == label_b   ifelse(     agree, label_a,     # raw evidence outranks either label     ifelse(!is.na(raw_appointment), "Included (raw: appointment exists)",     ifelse(!is.na(raw_contacted) & raw_contacted == "No", "Excluded (raw: not contacted)",            ifelse(!is.na(label_a), label_a, label_b)))   ) }  demo <- data.frame(   call_id  = c("C01", "C02", "C03"),   label_a  = c("Included", "Excluded", "Included"),   label_b  = c("Included", "Included", "Excluded"),   raw_appt = as.Date(c("2019-07-15", "2019-07-20", NA)),   raw_contact = c("Yes", "Yes", "No") ) demo$canonical <- adjudicate(demo$raw_appt, demo$raw_contact, demo$label_a, demo$label_b) demo[, c("call_id", "label_a", "label_b", "canonical")] #>   call_id  label_a  label_b                          canonical #> 1     C01 Included Included                           Included #> 2     C02 Excluded Included Included (raw: appointment exists) #> 3     C03 Included Excluded      Excluded (raw: not contacted)

text: National Provider Identifier (NPI) numbers primary join key across downstream tables. Bad NPIs must caught early — row wrong NPI silently match wrong physician every subsequent lookup. mysterycall_validate_npi() applies three checks order: Strip non-digit characters leading/trailing whitespace. Require exactly 10 digits. Validate Luhn checksum (algorithm NPI standard mandates). rows npi_is_valid == TRUE survive. returned data frame strict subset input — rows ever added.

title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
text: Mystery-caller studies assemble provider rosters several upstream sources (NPPES, CMS Care Compare, internal call logs) carry formatting quirks. Three categories data-quality problems arise repeatedly: Phone numbers — formatting noise ((303) 555-1234, 303.555.1234, +13035551234) area codes don’t match provider’s reported state. Physician names — single free-text name field must split first / middle / last / suffix components used call scripts de-duplication logic. Table joins — silent row multiplication right-hand table unique join key, silent data loss large fraction left-hand rows find match right. vignette walks mysterycall helpers address problem. code runs without API keys using built-package data.

what: The problem with silent join failures
title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
text: plain dplyr::left_join() silently: Multiply rows right-hand key unique (many--one match becomes many--many). Drop rows join key types don’t match (e.g., integer vs. character NPI), causing every row land unmatched group. Return warning 40 % left-hand NPIs match right. mysterycall_safe_*_join() family wraps dplyr joins pre- post-join assertions make failures loud.

title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
code: calls <- data.frame(   npi  = c("1111111111", "2222222222", "3333333333"),   date = as.Date(c("2025-01-10", "2025-01-11", "2025-01-12")),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  demographics <- data.frame(   npi    = c("1111111111", "2222222222"),   gender = c("Female", "Male"),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  # 2 of 3 left rows match → coverage = 66.7 % < 95 % threshold → error tryCatch(   suppressMessages(mysterycall_safe_left_join(     left         = calls,     right        = demographics,     by           = "npi",     label_left   = "call_log",     label_right  = "demographics",     min_coverage = 0.95   )),   error = function(e) message("Caught: ", conditionMessage(e)) ) #> Caught: Join coverage 66.7% below 95.0% threshold -- lost 1 rows. call_log -> demographics on npi.  # Lower threshold to match the actual coverage result <- suppressMessages(mysterycall_safe_left_join(   left         = calls,   right        = demographics,   by           = "npi",   label_left   = "call_log",   label_right  = "demographics",   min_coverage = 0.60 )) result #>          npi       date gender #> 1 1111111111 2025-01-10 Female #> 2 2222222222 2025-01-11   Male #> 3 3333333333 2025-01-12   <NA>

what: 4. Putting it together: a complete roster QA pipeline
title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
text: built-physicians dataset contains 4,659 OBGYN subspecialists NPI name. block demonstrates full data-quality pipeline without API calls.
code: library(dplyr) #>  #> Attaching package: 'dplyr' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #>  #>     filter, lag #> The following objects are masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union  # ── 1. Parse physician names ────────────────────────────────────────────────── roster <- mysterycall::physicians |>   select(NPI, name, subspecialty)  parsed_names <- mysterycall_parse_physician_name(roster$name) roster <- bind_cols(roster, parsed_names)  low_conf <- filter(roster, parse_confidence == "low") message(sprintf("%d name(s) flagged as low-confidence (%.1f%%)",                 nrow(low_conf), 100 * nrow(low_conf) / nrow(roster))) #> 0 name(s) flagged as low-confidence (0.0%)  # ── 2. Validate parsed names ────────────────────────────────────────────────── validated_names <- mysterycall_validate_parsed_names(parsed_names) issues <- filter(validated_names, !is.na(quality_issue)) message(sprintf("%d name quality issue(s) detected:", nrow(issues))) #> 21 name quality issue(s) detected: print(table(issues$quality_issue)) #>  #> last_name_suspiciously_short      name_particle_in_middle  #>                           19                            2  # ── 3. Illustrate a safe join with a synthetic demographics sidecar ─────────── # In a real study this would be CMS Care Compare or similar demographics_sidecar <- data.frame(   NPI    = roster$NPI[1:4000],       # 4,000 of 4,659 have demographics   gender = sample(c("Female", "Male", "Unknown"),                   4000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.7, .28, .02)),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  roster_enriched <- suppressMessages(   mysterycall_safe_left_join(     left         = roster,     right        = demographics_sidecar,     by           = "NPI",     label_left   = "physicians",     label_right  = "demographics_sidecar",     min_coverage = 0.85   # expect ≥ 85 % match rate   ) )  # Coverage summary cat(sprintf(   "Roster rows: %d  |  Enriched rows: %d  |  Coverage: %.1f%%\n",   nrow(roster), nrow(roster_enriched),   100 * mean(!is.na(roster_enriched$gender)) )) #> Roster rows: 4659  |  Enriched rows: 4659  |  Coverage: 85.9%

what: Step 5: Join the Data to the Block Groups
title: Getting Data from the US Census Bureau for Isochrones
text: Load block group shapefile sf::st_read() join demographic table 12-character GEOID. Always join GEOID rather human-readable NAME column, name strings differ across ACS vintages (e.g. county name capitalization changes). Use mysterycall_safe_left_join() catch GEOID type mismatches (integer vs. character) verify coverage — every block group demographic table find matching geometry.
code: # Load the block group shapefile (replace path with your actual file) bg_shape <- sf::st_read("data/shp/block_group/") |>   dplyr::select(GEOID, geometry)  # Coerce GEOID to character on both sides before joining demographics_bg$geoid <- as.character(demographics_bg$geoid) bg_shape$GEOID        <- as.character(bg_shape$GEOID)  # Safe join: errors if < 99 % of demographic rows find a geometry match bg_with_geometry <- mysterycall_safe_left_join(   left         = demographics_bg,   right        = bg_shape,   by           = c("geoid" = "GEOID"),   label_left   = "demographics_bg",   label_right  = "block_group_shapefile",   min_coverage = 0.99 )  # Convert the joined data frame to an sf object bg_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(bg_with_geometry)  # Save the spatial object for the isochrone intersection step sf::st_write(bg_sf, "data/block_groups_with_demographics.gpkg", delete_dsn = TRUE) readr::write_rds(bg_sf, "data/block_groups_with_demographics.rds")

title: Getting Started with mysterycall
text: Finally, run Poisson regression robust standard errors analyze primary outcome (appointment acceptance rate).
code: # Fit a Poisson mixed model: subspecialty as random intercept allows # the demo model to converge with this small simulated sample. model <- mysterycall_poisson_model(   data             = results,   outcome          = "accepted",   predictors       = "insurance_scenario",   random_intercept = "subspecialty" ) #> 24 row(s) have accepted = 0 (same-day appointments). Poisson handles zeros; verify these are intentional. #> Fitting Poisson GLMER: accepted ~ insurance_scenario + (1 | subspecialty) #> boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Convergence issues detected: #>   boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Consider simplifying predictors or using nAGQ = 1. #> Singular fit: random-intercept variance is ~0. The physician-level random effect explains little variation. #> Model fitted: n=50, physicians=6, AIC=84.2, overdispersion=0.50  # Print the incidence rate ratios (IRR) print(model) #> Poisson GLMER  n = 50  physicians = 6  AIC = 84.2  BIC = 89.9 #>   Warning: convergence warnings; singular fit #>   Reference levels: insurance_scenario='Medicaid' #>  #> Fixed effects (IRR with Wald CI): #>                        term   irr ci_lower ci_upper p_value_fmt #> 1               (Intercept) 0.259    0.124    0.544     < 0.001 #> 2 insurance_scenarioPrivate 3.186    1.340    7.579       0.009 #>  #> Random intercept (subspecialty):  variance = 0.0000  SD = 0.0000  # Generate a manuscript-ready results paragraph mysterycall_write_results_paragraph(   model_result = model,   ref_group = "Private",   exposure_col = "insurance_scenario",   outcome_label = "appointment acceptance" ) #> [1] "In multivariable Poisson regression, insurance_scenario was significantly associated with appointment acceptance (see Table X). Compared with Private, callers presenting as Private had an IRR of 3.19 (95% CI 1.34 to 7.58; p = 0.009) for appointment acceptance."

code: business_days <- function(from, to, holidays = as.Date(character(0))) {   vapply(seq_along(from), function(i) {     if (is.na(from[i]) || is.na(to[i]) || to[i] < from[i]) return(NA_real_)     if (to[i] == from[i]) return(0)     d <- seq(from[i] + 1, to[i], by = "day")     sum(!(format(d, "%u") %in% c("6", "7")) & !(d %in% holidays))   }, numeric(1)) }  calls$call_date <- as.Date(c("2019-07-01", "2019-07-01", "2019-07-02",                              "2019-07-02", "2019-07-03",                              "2019-07-08", "2019-07-08", "2019-07-09", "2019-07-09")) calls$wait_derived <- business_days(calls$call_date, calls$appointment_date,                                     holidays = as.Date("2019-07-04")) calls[, c("clinic", "call_date", "appointment_date", "wait_derived")] #>       clinic  call_date appointment_date wait_derived #> 1  Northside 2019-07-01       2019-07-11            7 #> 2   Lakeview 2019-07-01             <NA>           NA #> 3     Harbor 2019-07-02             <NA>           NA #> 4 Cedar Park 2019-07-02       2019-08-23           37 #> 5   Ridgeway 2019-07-03             <NA>           NA #> 6     Summit 2019-07-08       2019-09-03           41 #> 7   Fairmont 2019-07-08             <NA>           NA #> 8  Brookline 2019-07-09             <NA>           NA #> 9   Eastgate 2019-07-09             <NA>           NA mysterycall_guard_contaminated_wait(   data.frame(appointment_date = calls$appointment_date,              business_days_until_appointment = calls$wait_derived),   appointment_col = "appointment_date" )

what: 1. When to use LMM vs. Poisson/NB GLMM
title: Linear Mixed Models for Wait-Time Analysis
text: Mystery-caller studies collect wait times counts days call date offered appointment date. Two model families cover scenarios: function diagnoses distribution automatically: Skewness > 1 outcome ≥ 0: auto_log = TRUE (default) applies log1p(wait_days) fitting, back-transforms results geometric mean ratios (GMRs) reporting. Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.05 residuals: warning issued , sensitivity_poisson = "auto" (default), Poisson GLMM run alongside LMM robustness check.

title: Linear Mixed Models for Wait-Time Analysis
text: examples use synthetic dataset resembling two-wave mystery-caller study comparing Medicaid commercial insurance patients across 20 physician practices.
code: set.seed(42) n_physicians <- 20 n_calls      <- 4     # calls per physician (2 insurance types × 2 call dates)  sim_data <- data.frame(   physician  = rep(paste0("Dr", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_physicians)), each = n_calls),   insurance  = rep(c("Medicaid", "Medicaid", "BCBS", "BCBS"), n_physicians),   wave       = rep(c("Wave1", "Wave2", "Wave1", "Wave2"), n_physicians),   # Medicaid callers wait ~8 days longer on average   wait_days  = round(pmax(0,     rnorm(n_physicians * n_calls,           mean = ifelse(rep(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE), n_physicians), 29, 21),           sd   = 10)   )),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) # Add a business-days column (≈ 5/7 of calendar days) sim_data$business_days <- round(sim_data$wait_days * 0.71)  head(sim_data) #>   physician insurance  wave wait_days business_days #> 1      Dr01  Medicaid Wave1        43            31 #> 2      Dr01  Medicaid Wave2        23            16 #> 3      Dr01      BCBS Wave1        25            18 #> 4      Dr01      BCBS Wave2        27            19 #> 5      Dr02  Medicaid Wave1        33            23 #> 6      Dr02  Medicaid Wave2        28            20

text: satisfy M&M promise supplemental table comparing calendar-day business-day wait times, use mysterycall_calendar_sensitivity(): comparison table: Whether term directions consistent across measurement approaches: ready--paste supplemental paragraph:
code: sens <- mysterycall_calendar_sensitivity(   data             = sim_data,   calendar_col     = "wait_days",   business_col     = "business_days",   predictors       = c("insurance", "wave"),   random_intercept = "physician",   ref_label        = "BCBS (commercial)",   supp_table_num   = "S2" ) #> Fitting calendar-days model (wait_days)... #> Fitting business-days model (business_days)... sens$summary_table #>                Term                 Calendar days                 Business days #> 1 insuranceMedicaid  7.9 (3.3 to 12.6), p = 0.001     5.7 (2.4 to 9), p = 0.001 #> 2         waveWave2 -0.5 (-5.2 to 4.1), p = 0.822 -0.5 (-3.8 to 2.8), p = 0.775 #>   Consistent #> 1        Yes #> 2        Yes sens$all_consistent #> [1] TRUE cat(sens$paragraph) #> As a pre-specified sensitivity analysis, we repeated the secondary wait-time analysis substituting business days (Monday through Friday, excluding the 11 U.S. federal holidays) for calendar days. Business days were computed using the R package \emph{bizdays} with a US Federal holiday calendar. The calendar-day model included 80 observations with a recorded appointment date; the business-day model included 80 observations. Both models used the same mixed-effects linear regression specification (insurance and wave as fixed effect compared with BCBS (commercial) (reference); physician practice as random intercept). Results were directionally consistent across both metrics for all comparisons. Business-day estimates were on average 81% of calendar-day estimates (median ratio = 0.81), consistent with the expected 5/7 weekday fraction. Shapiro-Wilk normality tests on model residuals: calendar-day model: W = 0.985, p = 0.499; business-day model: W = 0.987, p = 0.595. Full results are presented in Supplemental Table S2.

title: Designing a matched-control mystery-caller audit
text: simulate 60 private-equity-owned (“treated”) practices concentrated three metros, plus large pool independent candidate controls metros. practice carries covariates want balance — years practice, physician gender, degree (MD vs ) — city/state. treated practices drawn slightly younger often -led, arms balanced begin .
code: set.seed(2026) metros <- list(   CO = c("Denver", "Aurora", "Lakewood"),   TX = c("Dallas", "Irving", "Plano"),   FL = c("Miami", "Hialeah", "Miami Beach") ) draw <- function(n, treated) {   st <- sample(names(metros), n, TRUE)   data.frame(     npi   = NA_integer_,     state = st,     city  = vapply(st, function(s) sample(metros[[s]], 1), character(1)),     years = round(rpois(n, if (treated) 11 else 12)),     female = rbinom(n, 1, if (treated) 0.45 else 0.55),     md = rbinom(n, 1, if (treated) 0.72 else 0.82),     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   ) } treated    <- draw(60, TRUE);   treated$npi    <- 1:60 candidates <- draw(600, FALSE); candidates$npi <- 1001:1600 head(treated) #>   npi state     city years female md #> 1   1    CO   Denver     6      0  1 #> 2   2    CO Lakewood     5      1  0 #> 3   3    CO Lakewood     6      0  0 #> 4   4    TX   Dallas    10      1  1 #> 5   5    CO   Aurora     8      1  0 #> 6   6    FL    Miami    16      1  0

title: Designing a matched-control mystery-caller audit
text: Matching rests propensity score — modeled probability treated given covariates. mysterycall_build_matched_controls() fits internally, worth inspecting. model, fit directly: Matching works treated control scores overlap (common-support assumption). treated practice score control comes close honest match. code: ps_df <- rbind(cbind(treatment = 1, treated[, c("years", "female", "md")]),                cbind(treatment = 0, candidates[, c("years", "female", "md")])) ps_fit <- glm(treatment ~ years + female + md, binomial, ps_df) round(coef(summary(ps_fit)), 3) #>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) #> (Intercept)   -0.420      0.528  -0.796    0.426 #> years         -0.132      0.043  -3.086    0.002 #> female        -0.397      0.274  -1.447    0.148 #> md            -0.223      0.323  -0.689    0.491 treated$ps    <- predict(ps_fit, treated, type = "response") candidates$ps <- predict(ps_fit, candidates, type = "response") library(ggplot2) ggplot(mapping = aes(x = ps)) +   geom_density(data = candidates, aes(fill = "Candidate pool"), alpha = 0.5) +   geom_density(data = treated, aes(fill = "Treated (PE)"), alpha = 0.5) +   scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c("Candidate pool" = "grey70",                                      "Treated (PE)" = "#08519c")) +   labs(x = "Propensity score", y = "Density",        title = "Propensity-score overlap between arms") +   theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top")

what: 6. Did matching work? Balance before and after
title: Designing a matched-control mystery-caller audit
text: point matching erase covariate imbalance built . Compare standardized mean difference (SMD) covariate matching (treated vs. whole candidate pool) (treated vs. matched controls). SMD 0.1 usual “well-balanced” rule thumb. Every covariate moves toward zero matching.
code: smd <- function(a, b) {   (mean(a) - mean(b)) / sqrt((var(a) + var(b)) / 2) } before <- vapply(c("years", "female", "md"),                  function(v) smd(treated[[v]], candidates[[v]]), numeric(1)) after  <- setNames(m$balance$smd, m$balance$covariate) round(data.frame(before_matching = before, after_matching = after[names(before)]), 3) #>        before_matching after_matching #> years           -0.451          0.000 #> female          -0.190         -0.033 #> md              -0.153          0.000

title: A matched-pair mystery-caller analysis
text: simulate 140 practices, called twice (Commercial Medicaid), per-practice random effect two calls one practice correlated. data long form: one row per practice × scenario. make data-integrity tools earn keep, deliberately introduce two kinds contradiction creep real call logs:
code: set.seed(2026) np <- 140L  subspecialty <- sample(c("General", "Pediatric", "Rhinology", "Laryngology"),                        np, TRUE, prob = c(.45, .25, .18, .12)) region <- sample(c("Northeast", "South", "Midwest", "West"), np, TRUE) caller <- sample(paste0("RA", 1:5), np, TRUE) u      <- rnorm(np, 0, 0.7)                              # practice generosity cbsa   <- ifelse(runif(np) < 0.72,                  sprintf("C%05d", sample(10000:40000, np, TRUE)), NA_character_) cfips  <- sprintf("%05d", sample(1001:56045, np, TRUE))  d <- data.frame(   practice = rep(seq_len(np), times = 2L),   scenario = rep(c("Commercial", "Medicaid"), each = np),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) d$subspecialty <- subspecialty[d$practice] d$region       <- region[d$practice] d$caller       <- caller[d$practice] d$cbsa_code    <- cbsa[d$practice] d$county_fips  <- cfips[d$practice]  medicaid <- d$scenario == "Medicaid" sub_off  <- c(General = 0, Pediatric = -0.3, Rhinology = 0.2, Laryngology = 0.1) eta      <- 1.1 - 1.0 * medicaid + u[d$practice] + sub_off[d$subspecialty]  d$office_answered     <- runif(nrow(d)) < 0.94 d$appointment_offered <- d$office_answered & (runif(nrow(d)) < plogis(eta)) d$taking_new_patients <- ifelse(d$appointment_offered | runif(nrow(d)) < 0.6,                                 "Yes", "No")  sub_wait <- c(General = 0, Pediatric = 0.15, Rhinology = 0.1, Laryngology = 0.2) mu_wait  <- exp(2.4 + 0.45 * medicaid + sub_wait[d$subspecialty]) d$wait_days_business <- ifelse(   d$appointment_offered, rnbinom(nrow(d), mu = mu_wait, size = 2), NA_real_)  d$appointment_outcome <- ifelse(   d$appointment_offered,   sample(c("With sampled physician", "With different physician"),          nrow(d), TRUE, c(.8, .2)),   "No appointment offered")  # a `complete` flag: a handful of calls never reached a determination d$complete <- d$office_answered | runif(nrow(d)) < 0.5  head(d) #>   practice   scenario subspecialty    region caller cbsa_code county_fips #> 1        1 Commercial    Pediatric      West    RA1    C18767       50173 #> 2        2 Commercial    Pediatric Northeast    RA4    C14100       30599 #> 3        3 Commercial      General   Midwest    RA5    C30688       34473 #> 4        4 Commercial      General   Midwest    RA2    C18966       46502 #> 5        5 Commercial    Pediatric Northeast    RA3    C31877       25887 #> 6        6 Commercial      General Northeast    RA5      <NA>       53447 #>   office_answered appointment_offered taking_new_patients wait_days_business #> 1           FALSE               FALSE                 Yes                 NA #> 2           FALSE               FALSE                 Yes                 NA #> 3            TRUE                TRUE                 Yes                  4 #> 4           FALSE               FALSE                  No                 NA #> 5            TRUE               FALSE                 Yes                 NA #> 6            TRUE                TRUE                 Yes                  5 #>      appointment_outcome complete #> 1 No appointment offered     TRUE #> 2 No appointment offered    FALSE #> 3 With sampled physician     TRUE #> 4 No appointment offered    FALSE #> 5 No appointment offered     TRUE #> 6 With sampled physician     TRUE # (a) a wait time recorded even though no appointment was offered d$appointment_offered[5]  <- FALSE d$appointment_outcome[5]  <- "No appointment offered" d$wait_days_business[5]   <- 14  # (b) the offered flag disagrees with the authoritative outcome d$appointment_offered[8]  <- FALSE                       # title: A matched-pair mystery-caller analysis
text: Access audits two-part outcome — binary offer full sample wait time among offered calls — parts must powered. mysterycall_twopart_power() simulates . simulation-based power sanity-checked calibration — rejection rate null must sit near α. mysterycall_type_i_check() turns observed null-rejection count verdict: mysterycall_find_mde() bisects power function smallest detectable effect target power — smallest Medicaid wait (days) detectable 80% power 400 calls: study oversamples rare stratum wants population-generalizable effect, mysterycall_marginal_power() powers post-stratification-weighted marginal estimand (needs glmmTMB marginaleffects):
code: mysterycall_twopart_power(   n_total = c(200, 400), offer_ref = 0.75, offer_trt = 0.55,   wait_ref = 14, wait_trt = 21, phi = 1.7, n_sim = 60, seed = 1) #> <mysterycall two-part power: 2 sample size(s), 60 sims, alpha 0.050> #> # A tibble: 2 × 8 #>   n_total n_ref n_trt pow_offer pow_wait mean_offered convergence_rate n_sim #>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>            <dbl> <dbl> #> 1     200   100   100     0.783    0.817         130.                1    60 #> 2     400   200   200     1        0.967         260.                1    60 mysterycall_type_i_check(rejections = 4, n_sim = 100, alpha = 0.05) #> # A tibble: 1 × 6 #>   rejection_rate ci_low ci_high n_sim alpha_in_ci verdict                       #>            <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>       <chr>                         #> 1           0.04 0.0110  0.0993   100 TRUE        consistent with nominal alpha pf <- function(wait_trt) {   mysterycall_twopart_power(     n_total = 400, offer_ref = 0.7, offer_trt = 0.7,     wait_ref = 14, wait_trt = wait_trt, phi = 1.7, n_sim = 30, seed = 1   )$table$pow_wait } mysterycall_find_mde(pf, lower = 14, upper = 26, target_power = 0.80,                      tol = 0.5, max_iter = 8)$mde #> [1] 18.5 mysterycall_marginal_power(   n_subject = c(150, 300),   cell_means = c(14, 18, 17, 24),      # Commercial/Medicaid x urban/rural waits   sigma_subject = 0.4, phi = 1.7,   stratum_sampling = 0.5, pop_stratum = 0.15,   n_sim = 200, seed = 1)

title: Mystery Caller Workflow: From Raw Data to Manuscript
text: Mystery-caller (secret-shopper) studies measure disparities healthcare access trained callers pose patients requesting appointments different insurance types. physician sampling frame called per insurance type; caller records whether appointment offered , , many business days earliest available slot. mysterycall package provides structured pipeline raw call logs manuscript-ready statistics, covering quality control, deduplication, descriptive summaries, regression modeling, sensitivity analyses.

title: Mystery Caller Workflow: From Raw Data to Manuscript
text: construct 200-row data frame representing 100 physician offices, called twice — Medicaid Blue Cross/Blue Shield.
code: suppressMessages({   library(mysterycall)    set.seed(42)   n_phy  <- 100L   ids    <- sprintf("%03d", seq_len(n_phy))   phones <- paste0("555-", sprintf("%04d", seq_len(n_phy)))    raw_df <- data.frame(     id_number             = rep(ids, each = 2L),     phone                 = rep(phones, each = 2L),     physician_information = paste0("Dr. Physician ", rep(ids, each = 2L)),     insurance             = rep(c("Medicaid", "Blue Cross/Blue Shield"), n_phy),     stringsAsFactors      = FALSE   )    raw_df$reason_for_exclusions <- sample(     c("Able to contact", "Physician not available", "Number disconnected"),     200L, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.70, 0.20, 0.10)   )    # Appointment wait times only for successfully-contacted rows   raw_df$business_days_until_appointment <- ifelse(     raw_df$reason_for_exclusions == "Able to contact",     rpois(200L, lambda = 14L) + 1L,     NA_integer_   )    # Medicaid acceptance column: realistic for Medicaid rows, boilerplate for BCBS   medicaid_vals <- sample(     c(       "Yes they accept Medicaid",       "No",       "No answer, unable to determine if they accept Medicaid."     ),     200L, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.30, 0.15)   )   raw_df$does_the_physician_accept_medicaid <- ifelse(     raw_df$insurance == "Medicaid",     medicaid_vals,     "NA as this was a Blue Cross/Blue Shield call."   )    raw_df$scenario <- sample(     c("HIP scenario", "SHOULDER scenario", "KNEE scenario"),     200L, replace = TRUE   )   raw_df$gender <- sample(c("Male", "Female"), 200L, replace = TRUE)   raw_df$state  <- sample(     c(       "Colorado", "Texas", "California", "New York", "Florida",       "Illinois", "Pennsylvania", "Ohio", "Georgia", "Michigan"     ),     200L, replace = TRUE   )   raw_df$notes <- NA_character_ })  dim(raw_df) #> [1] 200  11 head(raw_df[, c("id_number", "phone", "insurance",                 "reason_for_exclusions", "business_days_until_appointment")]) #>   id_number    phone              insurance   reason_for_exclusions #> 1       001 555-0001               Medicaid     Number disconnected #> 2       001 555-0001 Blue Cross/Blue Shield     Number disconnected #> 3       002 555-0002               Medicaid         Able to contact #> 4       002 555-0002 Blue Cross/Blue Shield Physician not available #> 5       003 555-0003               Medicaid         Able to contact #> 6       003 555-0003 Blue Cross/Blue Shield         Able to contact #>   business_days_until_appointment #> 1                              NA #> 2                              NA #> 3                              11 #> 4                              NA #> 5                              12 #> 6                              13

code: wt_grp <- suppressMessages(   mysterycall_wait_time_by_group(     df,     group_col  = "insurance",     output_dir = NA   ) ) print(wt_grp) #> # A tibble: 2 × 5 #>   insurance              median_days    q1    q3     n #>   <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> #> 1 Blue Cross/Blue Shield        14.5    12    17    64 #> 2 Medicaid                      14      11    17    65  wt_sent <- suppressMessages(   mysterycall_wait_time_sentence(df, group_col = "insurance") ) cat(wt_sent$sentence, "\n") #> The median wait time across all insurance was 14 business days (IQR: 11 to 17). Specifically, the median wait time was 14 days (IQR: 12 to 17) for Blue Cross/Blue Shield, 14 days (IQR: 11 to 17) for Medicaid. The p-value for Medicaid vs Blue Cross/Blue Shield was 0.900.

title: Pipeline Guarantees
text: silent row loss: mysterycall_clean_phase1() never silently drops rows. Rows flagged issues (empty name, duplicate, etc.) marked processing_flag_* columns retained output unless remove_duplicates = TRUE explicitly set. NPI integrity: mysterycall_validate_npi() removes rows whose NPI NA, non-10-digit, fails Luhn checksum. never adds rows. Output NPI column always character type. Zero-row safety: mysterycall_search_taxonomy() returns zero-row data frame (never NULL) registry records match taxonomy description network unavailable retries. Workload completeness: mysterycall_split_and_save() assigns every input row exactly one assistant’s workbook via round-robin; row omitted duplicated across workbooks.

title: Pipeline Guarantees
text: NPI registry retries: mysterycall_search_taxonomy() retries failed HTTP requests 3 times exponential back-(1 s, 2 s, 4 s). retries fail, function logs warning returns empty data frame; throw error. Missing package handling: optional dependencies (mapping, Excel /O, progress bars, etc.) guarded requireNamespace(..., quietly = TRUE). Functions degrade gracefully: map functions skip rendering; progress bars fall back message() output; Excel export falls back CSV. Workflow isolation: mysterycall_run_workflow() wraps pipeline stage tryCatch. failure Phase 2 cleaning prevent Phase 1 output written returned.

Power curves — required sample size change across range effect sizes? functions shown power analysis family:

title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies

title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies
text: sampling frame known, finite directory NN providers, Cochran (1977) formula gives minimum sample nn estimated proportion (e.g. acceptance rate) within ee percentage points 95 % confidence: n0=Zα/22⋅p(1−p)e2→n=n01+n0−1N n_0 = \frac{Z^2_{\alpha/2} \cdot p(1-p)}{e^2} \qquad\longrightarrow\qquad n = \frac{n_0}{1 + \frac{n_0 - 1}{N}} Setting p=0.5p = 0.5 (maximum variance) Z0.025=1.96Z_{0.025} = 1.96 simplifies : n=N1+Ne2 n = \frac{N}{1 + N e^2} finite-population correction factor (1+n0−1N)−1\left(1 + \frac{n_0-1}{N}\right)^{-1} makes n<n0n < n_0 whenever sample represents meaningful fraction directory.

title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies
text: Required sample sizes across directory sizes precision targets. Key insight: moderate--large directories (N ≥ 400), ±5% target requires roughly 200 providers regardless large directory grows — finite-population correction becomes negligible.
code: # 800 OB-GYNs in target region — need acceptance rate within ±5 percentage points res_800 <- mysterycall_cochran_n(N = 800, margin_of_error = 0.05) cat(sprintf(   "N = %d providers, target ME ±%.0f%%: sample n = %d (achieved ME = ±%.1f%%)\n",   res_800$N, res_800$margin_of_error * 100,   res_800$n, res_800$effective_margin * 100 )) #> N = 800 providers, target ME ±5%: sample n = 267 (achieved ME = ±5.0%) # Show how n changes across directory sizes and margin-of-error targets grid <- expand.grid(   N  = c(100, 200, 400, 800, 1600),   me = c(0.03, 0.05, 0.10) )  grid$n <- mapply(   function(N, me) mysterycall_cochran_n(N, me)$n,   grid$N, grid$me )  pivot_tbl <- stats::reshape(   grid,   idvar = "N", timevar = "me", direction = "wide" ) names(pivot_tbl) <- c("Directory size (N)", "n at ±3%", "n at ±5%", "n at ±10%")  knitr::kable(   pivot_tbl,   caption = "Required sample sizes across directory sizes and precision targets." )

title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies
text: Poisson power analysis: providers per arm paired design, lambda_ref = 14 days, alpha = 0.05. Interpretation: Detecting small IRR (1.20) requires substantially providers detecting large one (1.60+). paired design (provider called insurance types) halves total providers compared independent-groups design. Increasing power 80 % 90 % adds roughly 25–35 % providers.
code: scenarios <- list(   list(irr = 1.20, power = 0.80, label = "Small effect (IRR 1.20), 80% power"),   list(irr = 1.40, power = 0.80, label = "Moderate effect (IRR 1.40), 80% power"),   list(irr = 1.40, power = 0.90, label = "Moderate effect (IRR 1.40), 90% power"),   list(irr = 1.60, power = 0.80, label = "Large effect (IRR 1.60), 80% power"),   list(irr = 2.00, power = 0.80, label = "Very large effect (IRR 2.00), 80% power") )  pw_rows <- lapply(scenarios, function(s) {   res <- mysterycall_poisson_power(     irr        = s$irr,     lambda_ref = 14,     power      = s$power,     both_arms  = TRUE   )   data.frame(     Scenario       = s$label,     IRR            = s$irr,     Power          = sprintf("%.0f%%", s$power * 100),     `n per arm`    = res$n_per_arm,     `Total providers` = res$n_total,     `Total calls`  = res$n_total_calls,     check.names    = FALSE   ) }) #> Poisson power: IRR=1.20, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=16.8 | n_per_arm=31, n_total=31, calls=62 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=19.6 | n_per_arm=9, n_total=9, calls=18 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=19.6 | n_per_arm=12, n_total=12, calls=24 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.60, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=22.4 | n_per_arm=5, n_total=5, calls=10 #> Poisson power: IRR=2.00, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=28.0 | n_per_arm=2, n_total=2, calls=4  pw_tbl <- do.call(rbind, pw_rows)  knitr::kable(   pw_tbl,   caption = paste(     "Poisson power analysis: providers per arm for a paired design,",     "lambda_ref = 14 days, alpha = 0.05."   ) )

title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies
text: practice, providers practice share scheduling staff, calls office may correlated. design effect inflates sample size : DEFF=1+(m−1)×ρ \text{DEFF} = 1 + (m - 1) \times \rho mm average calls per cluster (office) ρ\rho intra-class correlation (ICC). Effect within-office correlation (ICC) required sample size. IRR = 1.40, lambda_ref = 14 d, 80% power, m = 3 calls/office. Rule thumb: ICC 0.10 3 calls per office inflates required sample ~20 %. ICC unknown, sensitivity analysis across ICC values (0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20) recommended.
code: # No clustering vs. ICC = 0.10 (moderate) with 3 calls per office on average pw_no_icc  <- mysterycall_poisson_power(irr = 1.40, lambda_ref = 14) #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=19.6 | n_per_arm=9, n_total=9, calls=18 pw_icc_010 <- mysterycall_poisson_power(irr = 1.40, lambda_ref = 14,                                          icc = 0.10, calls_per_cluster = 3) #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=19.6 | n_per_arm=11, n_total=11, calls=22 pw_icc_020 <- mysterycall_poisson_power(irr = 1.40, lambda_ref = 14,                                          icc = 0.20, calls_per_cluster = 3) #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=19.6 | n_per_arm=12, n_total=12, calls=24  icc_tbl <- data.frame(   ICC            = c("0 (none)", "0.10 (moderate)", "0.20 (high)"),   DEFF           = c(pw_no_icc$design_effect,                      pw_icc_010$design_effect,                      pw_icc_020$design_effect),   `n per arm`    = c(pw_no_icc$n_per_arm,                      pw_icc_010$n_per_arm,                      pw_icc_020$n_per_arm),   `Total calls`  = c(pw_no_icc$n_total_calls,                      pw_icc_010$n_total_calls,                      pw_icc_020$n_total_calls),   check.names    = FALSE )  knitr::kable(   icc_tbl,   digits  = 2,   caption = paste(     "Effect of within-office correlation (ICC) on required sample size.",     "IRR = 1.40, lambda_ref = 14 d, 80% power, m = 3 calls/office."   ) )

what: 6. Sample Size Across Reference Wait Times
title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies
text: expected wait time reference arm (lambda_ref) also affects required sample size. Studies different specialties regions adapt parameter. Required sample size per arm IRR = 1.40 across different reference wait-time assumptions. Interpretation: wait times get shorter (fewer days), Poisson rate becomes smaller variable relative mean, providers needed detect proportional difference.
code: lambda_vals <- c(5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 30)  n_by_lambda <- vapply(lambda_vals, function(lam)   mysterycall_poisson_power(irr = 1.40, lambda_ref = lam, power = 0.80,                              both_arms = TRUE)$n_per_arm,   numeric(1)) #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=5.0, lambda_trt=7.0 | n_per_arm=24, n_total=24, calls=48 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=7.0, lambda_trt=9.8 | n_per_arm=17, n_total=17, calls=34 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=10.0, lambda_trt=14.0 | n_per_arm=12, n_total=12, calls=24 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=19.6 | n_per_arm=9, n_total=9, calls=18 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=21.0, lambda_trt=29.4 | n_per_arm=6, n_total=6, calls=12 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=30.0, lambda_trt=42.0 | n_per_arm=4, n_total=4, calls=8  lam_df <- data.frame(lambda_ref = lambda_vals, n_per_arm = n_by_lambda)  ggplot(lam_df, aes(x = lambda_ref, y = n_per_arm)) +   geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", alpha = 0.8) +   geom_text(aes(label = n_per_arm), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +   labs(     title   = "Sample size sensitivity to reference wait time",     subtitle = "IRR = 1.40, 80% power, paired design",     x       = "Reference-arm mean wait time (days)",     y       = "Required providers per arm"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

text: USDA ERS publishes ZIP--RUCA crosswalk : https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-commuting-area-codes Download ZIP code file (census tract file). 2023, file named something like ruca2010revised.xlsx. what: Step 1: Load and clean the crosswalk
title: Provider Classification and Demographic Enrichment
text: Critical: Always read ZIP codes character, integer. ZIP codes like 01234 (Massachusetts) lose leading zero read numeric, causing New England providers fail join.
code: library(readr)  ruca_crosswalk <- read_csv(   "data-raw/ruca2010revised.csv",   col_types = cols(     ZIP_CODE = col_character(),  # keep leading zeros: "01234" not 1234     RUCA1    = col_double()   ) ) |>   dplyr::select(zip5 = ZIP_CODE, ruca_code = RUCA1) |>   dplyr::distinct(zip5, .keep_all = TRUE)  # one row per ZIP

title: Provider Classification and Demographic Enrichment

code: roster <- roster |>   dplyr::mutate(     zip5 = stringr::str_sub(addresses_postal_code, 1L, 5L)   )

title: Provider Classification and Demographic Enrichment
text: mysterycall_safe_left_join() performs several safety checks automatically: asserts ruca_crosswalk unique keys zip5 (duplicate ZIP rows fan roster). coerces mismatched column types (e.g., one side zip5 integer character) prevent silent zero-match joins. reports join coverage: fraction roster rows found matching ZIP crosswalk. stops informative error coverage falls min_coverage. coverage 90%, inspect unmatched ZIPs: Post office box ZIP codes, US territories (Guam, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands), military APO/FPO addresses common sources unmatched ZIPs. Decide advance whether providers excluded RUCA analysis assigned manual code.

text: National Provider Identifier (NPI) registry publish physician birth year. deliberate privacy protection. However, registry publish medical school graduation year, strong proxy age. mysterycall_impute_age() converts graduation year estimated current age using formula: age_offset (default 27) median age US medical school graduation. method validated Doximity birth-year data 32,000 OB/GYN physicians (r = 0.962, mean absolute error = 2.1 years) 348 ENT physicians (r = 0.957, MAE = 1.7 years).

code: roster <- roster |>   dplyr::mutate(     age_imputed = mysterycall_impute_age(       graduation_year,       ref_year   = 2023L,  # pin to your data collection year       age_offset = 27L     # validated median age at US med school graduation     )   )

Investigate proceeding. Implausible ages (min_age = 25 max_age = 90): Values outside range set NA warning. physician graduated 1924 computed age 129 2023 — almost certainly data entry error NPPES. Check rows manually.

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: mystery-caller study (also called audit study correspondence study) controlled experiment used detect discrimination health-care access. central idea elegantly simple: trained research callers—posing prospective patients—telephone physician offices attempt schedule new-patient appointment. callers follow standardized script, vary characteristic investigation (commonly insurance type), record outcome call, design provides direct, high-fidelity measure real-world access disparities surveys claims data replicate. method pioneered health disparities research Asplin colleagues (2005) since applied dozens specialty access questions: Medicaid patients wait longer orthopedic consultation? uninsured callers offered fewer -month appointments commercially insured callers? mysterycall package implements statistical routines needed answer questions correctly.

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: Every mystery-caller call produces exactly two outcomes capture different dimensions access: Appointment offered (binary, 0/1). office offer caller new-patient appointment ? value 0 means office declined, said accepting new patients, gave number disconnected never answered. value 1 means appointment scheduled offered. primary disparity outcome. Wait time business days (count ≥ 0). Among calls resulted offered appointment (appointment_offered == 1), many business days elapsed date call earliest available appointment? non-negative integer count analyzed Poisson generalized linear model. important understand two outcomes measure different barriers. Medicaid patient might face binary access barrier (turned away entirely) wait-time barrier (accepted, wait longer). reported; reporting one paints incomplete picture.

what: Within-Physician Correlation: Why Multilevel Models Are Essential
title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: critical design feature separates mystery-caller data simple cross-sectional surveys physician (identified National Provider Identifier, NPI) called multiple times different insurance types. typical study design calls physician Medicaid patient, privately insured patient, Medicare patient, uninsured patient—producing four observations per physician. means observations independent. Two calls physician share physician’s baseline acceptance behavior, scheduling culture, practice-level factors (urban vs. rural, solo vs. group practice, etc.). fit ordinary logistic Poisson regression treats every call independent observation, : Underestimate standard errors (effectively overcounting information data). Report confidence intervals narrow p-values small—inflating Type error rate. Fail separate within-physician insurance effect (physician behave differently depending calling?) -physician effect (high-Medicaid-accepting physicians differ systematically low-accepting physicians?). solution add physician-level random intercept model. random intercept absorbs physician’s baseline tendency offer appointments (baseline wait-time level), leaving fixed effects estimate pure insurance-type contrast within physicians. standard generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) approach, implemented R lme4 package.

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: Wait time business days count variable: takes non-negative integer values (0, 1, 2, 3, …), negative (physician offer appointment past), distribution typically right-skewed concentration small values long upper tail. properties disqualify ordinary least-squares linear regression primary analysis: Linear regression assumes continuous, symmetric, normally distributed outcome. Wait-time data violate three assumptions. Linear regression can predict negative wait times, nonsensical. equal-variance (homoscedasticity) assumption fails: variance wait times tends grow mean (Poisson processes variance = mean definition). text: ci_method argument supports three approaches: "wilson" (default): Wilson score interval preferred choice proportions. Unlike Wald interval (p̂±1.96SE\hat{p} \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}), Wilson interval always within [0,1][0, 1] excellent coverage probability even nn small true proportion near 0 1: p̃±zα/21+zα/22/np̂(1−p̂)n+zα/224n2,p̃=p̂+zα/22/(2n)1+zα/22/n\tilde{p} \pm \frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{1 + z_{\alpha/2}^2/n}   \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}{4n^2}}, \qquad   \tilde{p} = \frac{\hat{p} + z_{\alpha/2}^2/(2n)}{1 + z_{\alpha/2}^2/n} Use situations. - "exact" (Clopper-Pearson): exact binomial interval. guaranteed coverage ≥ 95 % cost conservative (wide). Use want conservative bound exact coverage guarantee matters (e.g., regulatory submissions). - "wald": standard normal approximation. Appropriate n ≥ 50 per group proportion 0.15 0.85. title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: Two corrections implemented mysterycall_multiple_comparison_adjust(): Bonferroni correction: Divide α\alpha threshold number tests mm (equivalently, multiply p-value mm, capping 1.0). adjusted p-value test kk : pkBonf=min⁡(m⋅pk,1)p_k^{\text{Bonf}} = \min(m \cdot p_k,\; 1) controls family-wise error rate exactly underpowered mm large. Holm-Bonferroni (Holm’s step-) correction: Sort raw p-values smallest largest: p(1)≤p(2)≤⋯≤p(m)p_{(1)} \le p_{(2)} \le \cdots \le p_{(m)}. adjusted p-value kk-th ordered test : p(k)Holm=min⁡(maxj≤k[(m−j+1)p(j)],1)p_{(k)}^{\text{Holm}} = \min\!\Bigl(\max_{j \le k}\!\bigl[(m - j + 1)\,p_{(j)}\bigr],\; 1\Bigr) Holm-Bonferroni uniformly powerful Bonferroni still controlling family-wise error rate. Prefer Holm-Bonferroni almost situations. Key insight output: Medicare comparison (raw p = 0.017) crosses Bonferroni-corrected threshold 0.017 (= 0.05/3) declared non-significant Bonferroni. However, remains significant Holm correction. illustrates Bonferroni can overly conservative: ignores ordering evidence across tests.
code: # Extract the raw p-values from the disparities table raw_p <- disparities$p_value names(raw_p) <- disparities$insurance[disparities$insurance != "Private"] raw_p #>    Medicaid    Medicare   Uninsured #>   < 0.0001      0.0170    < 0.0001  # Apply Bonferroni and Holm-Bonferroni corrections adj_results <- mysterycall_multiple_comparison_adjust(   p_values   = raw_p,   method     = c("bonferroni", "holm"),  # compute both   alpha      = 0.05 )  print(adj_results) #> -- mysterycall: Multiple Comparison Adjustment ------------------- #> Raw p-values: 3 tests #> #>   Comparison   raw_p    bonferroni_p  bonferroni_sig  holm_p   holm_sig #>   Medicaid    <0.001      <0.001          ***          <0.001     *** #>   Medicare     0.017       0.051           .            0.034      * #>   Uninsured   <0.001      <0.001          ***          <0.001     *** #> #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 #> #> Note: Holm correction is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni. #>       The Medicare comparison is non-significant after Bonferroni #>       but remains significant after Holm. Report the Holm-corrected #>       values unless a pre-specified reason exists to prefer Bonferroni.

code: # Example: bootstrap the ratio of median wait times (Medicaid / Private) # This has no closed-form CI, making bootstrap ideal.  set.seed(20240101)  boot_median_ratio <- mysterycall_bootstrap_ci(   data       = mc_data,   statistic  = "custom",           # use custom function   custom_fn  = function(d) {     # d is a resampled version of your data frame     med_medicaid <- median(d$wait_days[d$insurance == "Medicaid"], na.rm = TRUE)     med_private  <- median(d$wait_days[d$insurance == "Private"],  na.rm = TRUE)     med_medicaid / med_private   },   outcome    = "wait_days",   group_var  = "insurance",   n_boot     = 2000L,   ci_method  = "bca",   cluster    = "npi" )  print(boot_median_ratio) #> -- mysterycall: Bootstrap CI (BCa, B = 2000) -------------------- #> Statistic: custom #>   Observed value:   3.00  (median wait Medicaid: 19.5d, Private: 6.5d) #>   BCa 95% CI:     [2.17,  4.31] #> #> Interpretation: Medicaid patients' median wait time was 3.0 times longer #>   than privately insured patients' (BCa 95% CI: 2.2- to 4.3-fold).

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: Translating statistical output clear, accurate prose one time-consuming parts manuscript writing. function mysterycall_write_results_paragraph() accepts key model objects returns formatted results paragraph following APA 7th edition style conventions reporting guidelines JAMA NEJM observational health disparities research. APA-style formatting conventions used: - p-values expressed exact values (“p < 0.05” except p < 0.001) - 95 % CIs reported every effect estimate - Sample sizes stated upfront - Adjustment method named explicitly (“Holm-Bonferroni correction”) - Effect direction stated plain language (“waited 42% longer”) technical notation (IRR 1.42)
code: results_text <- mysterycall_write_results_paragraph(   poisson_model      = poisson_fit,   disparities_table  = adj_full,           # version with adjusted p-values   bootstrap_ci       = boot_result,   outcome_label      = "new-patient appointment",   insurance_ref      = "Private",   alpha              = 0.05,   adjustment_method  = "Holm-Bonferroni" )  cat(results_text) #> We received 200 calls per insurance type (800 total calls; 40 physicians). #> The overall appointment-offered rate was 91.0% (95% Wilson CI: 86.0%-94.5%) #> for privately insured callers, compared with 64.0% (95% CI: 57.2% to 70.3%) #> for Medicaid callers, 84.0% (95% CI: 78.1% to 88.8%) for Medicare callers, #> and 54.0% (95% CI: 47.1% to 60.8%) for uninsured callers. Medicaid callers #> were offered appointments at a rate 27.0 percentage points lower than #> privately insured callers (relative risk 0.70; 95% BCa bootstrap CI: #> -34.9 to -19.1 pp; Holm-adjusted p < .001). Uninsured callers had the #> lowest appointment-offered rate, 37.0 percentage points below the privately #> insured rate (relative risk 0.59; Holm-adjusted p < .001). Medicare callers #> had a 7.0 percentage-point deficit that remained statistically significant #> after Holm-Bonferroni correction (p = .034). #> #> Among callers offered appointments, we modelled wait time in business days #> using a Poisson generalized linear mixed-effects model with a physician-level #> random intercept to account for within-physician correlation (40 physicians; #> intraclass correlation coefficient 0.089). The Pearson chi-squared #> overdispersion ratio was 1.08, indicating adequate model fit. Medicaid #> callers waited 42% longer than privately insured callers (incidence rate #> ratio [IRR] 1.42; 95% profile-likelihood CI: 1.18-1.70; p < .001). #> Uninsured callers waited 29% longer (IRR 1.29; 95% CI: 1.06 to 1.57; p = .012). #> No statistically significant wait-time difference was observed for Medicare #> callers (IRR 1.08; 95% CI: 0.89 to 1.31; p = .441).

code: set.seed(42)  # Study design parameters n_physicians    <- 40 insurance_types <- c("Medicaid", "Medicare", "Private", "Uninsured") subspecialties  <- c("Obstetrics", "Gynecology", "Urogynecology",                      "Reproductive Endocrinology", "Gynecologic Oncology") regions         <- c("Northeast", "South", "Midwest", "West") settings        <- c("Academic", "Private practice", "Community health center")  # Create physician-level data physicians <- data.frame(   npi             = sprintf("%010d", seq_len(n_physicians)),   physician_gender = sample(c("Female", "Male"), n_physicians,                             replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.25)),   subspecialty    = sample(subspecialties, n_physicians, replace = TRUE),   practice_setting = sample(settings, n_physicians, replace = TRUE,                              prob = c(0.30, 0.50, 0.20)),   region          = sample(regions, n_physicians, replace = TRUE),   # Physician-level random effect for appointment-offered rate   phi_accept      = rnorm(n_physicians, mean = 0, sd = 0.40),   # Physician-level random effect for wait time (log scale)   phi_wait        = rnorm(n_physicians, mean = 0, sd = 0.30),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  # Create call-level data: each physician called once per insurance type calls_list <- lapply(seq_len(n_physicians), function(i) {   ph <- physicians[i, ]    # Insurance-type fixed effects on appointment-offered rate (log-odds scale)   # Reference = Private; Medicaid is hardest to get, Uninsured also hard   insurance_logodds <- c(     Medicaid  = -1.20,     Medicare  = -0.30,     Private   =  0.00,     Uninsured = -1.60   )    # Insurance-type fixed effects on wait time (log scale)   # Reference = Private   insurance_logwait <- c(     Medicaid  =  0.35,     Medicare  =  0.08,     Private   =  0.00,     Uninsured =  0.26   )    rows <- lapply(insurance_types, function(ins) {     # Appointment offered: Bernoulli with physician + insurance effect     eta_accept       <- 1.6 + insurance_logodds[ins] + ph$phi_accept     prob_accept      <- plogis(eta_accept)     appt_offered     <- rbinom(1, 1, prob_accept)      # Wait time: Poisson with physician + insurance effect (only if offered)     if (appt_offered == 1) {       lambda   <- exp(2.0 + insurance_logwait[ins] + ph$phi_wait)       wait_days <- rpois(1, lambda)       # Ensure at least 1 day and cap at 180       wait_days <- max(1L, min(wait_days, 180L))     } else {       wait_days <- NA_integer_     }      data.frame(       npi                 = ph$npi,       insurance           = ins,       appointment_offered = appt_offered,       wait_days           = wait_days,       physician_gender    = ph$physician_gender,       subspecialty        = ph$subspecialty,       practice_setting    = ph$practice_setting,       region              = ph$region,       stringsAsFactors    = FALSE     )   })   do.call(rbind, rows) })  mc_data <- do.call(rbind, calls_list) mc_data$insurance <- factor(mc_data$insurance,                              levels = c("Private", "Medicaid", "Medicare",                                         "Uninsured"))  # Verify dimensions dim(mc_data) #> [1] 160   8  # Show first six rows head(mc_data) #>          npi insurance appointment_offered wait_days physician_gender #>  0000000001  Private                   1        6         Female #>  0000000001  Medicaid                  0        NA        Female #>  0000000001  Medicare                  1        9         Female #>  0000000001  Uninsured                 0        NA        Female #>  0000000002  Private                   1        4           Male #>  0000000002  Medicaid                  1       14           Male #>    subspecialty practice_setting    region #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Gynecology  Academic          South #>     Gynecology  Academic          South
